premise.text: Seed terms: Utopia, Fundraiser, Sporting Event Stands / Bleachers, War breaking out, Kind, Melodramatic

fields.label: Laugh
fields.description: How likely a human reader is to actually laugh, not merely understand or admire the idea.

fields.label: Surprise
fields.description: Whether the turn avoids the first obvious route and lands with a satisfying snap.

fields.label: Craft
fields.description: Economy, stage rhythm, first-person clarity, escalation, and a final line that carries the laugh.

fields.label: Originality
fields.description: Freshness of comic angle, image, wording, and avoidance of familiar AI joke shapes.

fields.label: Prompt Fit
fields.description: Natural first-person stand-up form using exactly two seed terms as concepts, with the other four left out.

anchors.label: Broken
anchors.description: Not a joke, incoherent, unsafe, or unusable.

anchors.label: Weak
anchors.description: Recognizably attempting humor, but generic, strained, confusing, or mostly prompt recital.

anchors.label: Competent
anchors.description: Clear and publishable as filler, but unlikely to earn more than a mild smile.

anchors.label: Amusing
anchors.description: A real comic idea with a mild payoff; respectable, not a winner.

anchors.label: Good
anchors.description: A genuinely good joke with clear timing; some humans would repeat the comic idea or turn.

anchors.label: Excellent
anchors.description: Strong human-level joke with a memorable turn, clean construction, and no apologetic scoring curve.

anchors.label: Outstanding
anchors.description: Rare and replayable; clearly better than normal good AI humor and strong by human standards.

anchors.label: Classic
anchors.description: Reserve for a joke a human would quote later; most seasons should have none.

jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: The Fundraiser
jokes.joke: I went to a charity fundraiser where they auctioned off a dinner with a celebrity. The bidding got so intense, one woman stood up and screamed, 'I'll give you ten thousand dollars!' Everyone applauded. I leaned over and asked, 'Who's the celebrity?' She said, 'I don't know. That's my husband she's bidding on.'

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Bleacher Utopia
jokes.joke: I went to my nephew’s t-ball game, and I swear the other parents have never been more alive. A woman behind me screamed, ‘HE WAS SAFE! HE WAS SO SAFE!’ about a six-year-old who was lying down in the infield, eating a dandelion. She’s not a mother. She’s a Shakespearean widow in a folding chair. I clap politely for everything, because I peaked emotionally at the snack table.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: The Left Flank
jokes.joke: I was in the bleachers at my nephew’s under-eight soccer game. The score is zero to zero because both teams are just following a butterfly. But the parents are so melodramatic. One dad drops to his knees, screaming at the sky because his son Brayden failed to defend the left flank. Sir, Brayden is currently eating a handful of dirt. The only flank he’s defending is a fruit snack.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Little League Final Act
jokes.joke: I was up in the bleachers at my nephew’s little league game when one close call at the plate turned the dad next to me completely melodramatic. He stood up, threw his arms wide, and announced to the whole field, “This injustice will haunt our family for generations!” Meanwhile his kid was already back in the dugout asking for a snack.

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Charity Upgrade
jokes.joke: I went to a fundraiser where they auctioned off acts of kindness. I got caught up in the bidding and paid three hundred bucks for a stranger to help me move. The volunteer showed up, looked at my couch, and said, 'For three hundred, I can be kind or I can be honest.'

scores.comment: Strong visual contrast between parental hysteria and childhood obliviousness. The Shakespearean widow comparison is memorable and funny. The final snack-table line is amusing but weaker than the central image.
Accessible premise with effective visual absurdity. The military language adds comic contrast, but the butterfly and dirt-eating images are familiar. The final fruit-snack line feels somewhat forced.

Clear, economical setup and recognizable parental overreaction. However, the generational-injustice exaggeration is predictable, and the snack punchline merely reinforces the established contrast without a fresh turn.

Fresh fundraiser premise with a natural escalation and a concise conversational punchline. The distinction between kindness and honesty creates a satisfying turn, although the payoff is more wry than laugh-out-loud funny.
The twist is muddled: it’s unclear who is bidding on whom, so the final line doesn’t land. Melodramatic is barely used, and the celebrity-auction setup is familiar.

The butterfly-chasing 0-0 game is a nice image, and the flank/fruit snack callback closes cleanly. The melodramatic dad at a kids’ game is a familiar premise, and the ‘But the parents are so melodramatic’ line labels the joke instead of showing it.
’Haunt our family for generations’ is a good melodramatic line, but the kid-wants-a-snack ending is predictable and trails off instead of snapping. Reads more like an anecdote than a punchline.
Fresh premise of auctioning acts of kindness. The ‘kind or honest’ line is a clean, in-character insult about the couch and ends on the strongest beat.
The mechanics of the punchline are confusing and feel like a mangled street joke. It lacks the natural logic and flow required for a successful stand-up bit.
Excellent stand-up rhythm and escalation. The 'Shakespearean widow' line perfectly captures the melodramatic seed term in a concrete, performable way.
Competent but relies heavily on telling rather than showing the 'melodramatic' seed term. The punchline is mildly amusing but falls into a standard trope for youth sports jokes.
A clean, well-structured joke with a solid punchline about the universal misery of moving furniture. The seeds are integrated naturally into a believable stage premise.
Competent setup with a familiar husband-auction twist; the melodrama is only mild intensity and the final reveal is predictable.
Strong concrete image of the Shakespearean widow versus the dandelion-eating kid; clean first-person rhythm and a solid closing shrug.
Tight escalation from butterfly-chasing to dirt-eating; the fruit-snack flank line lands cleanly and carries the laugh.
Dry, efficient premise and a workable honesty punch; funny enough for a mild laugh but not especially surprising.
Clear setup and twist; husband reveal lands, though it's a familiar misdirection and melodramatic element is only lightly expressed.
Strong observational premise, vivid imagery, and a good closing tag. Melodrama concept is clear and naturally tied to the stands setting.
Good escalation from butterfly to dirt-eating child. The fruit-snack comparison is a solid punchline, though the overall angle is familiar.
Clean and understandable, but the joke follows the expected path and the snack contrast is a fairly predictable payoff.

featureImagePrompt:
Generate one polished web feature image for Paperclipalypse.
ASPECT RATIO: exactly 2:1, horizontal wide banner.
Style: full-color gothic newspaper-comic illustration, darkly funny but warm, clean black ink, crisp editorial cartoon linework, cinematic stage lighting, high contrast, readable composition. Not monochrome. Not sepia-only. Use a balanced color palette: warm amber stage lights, dark bronze and silver metal paperclip, muted greens for the joke setting, dusty blue-gray shadows, cream-white text, subtle deep red accent lights.
Composition instructions, not visible labels:
- Compose the image as one continuous illustration, not as a boxy triptych or three separate image panels. Do not add white gutters, hard section borders, or comic-strip dividers between the paperclip stage and the joke scenario.
- Let the paperclip stage on the left bleed visually into the joke scenario in the center through shared lighting, background, floor, props, or atmosphere. The right-side joke text may remain distinct inside its own dark framed poster panel.
- Put a charming anthropomorphic paperclip stand-up comedian at a vintage microphone on the left side of the image. The paperclip should look metallic and expressive, related to Paperclipalypse's paperclip-comedian logo, but not identical.
- Put the winning joke scene in the middle of the image, shown as literal visual comedy action and props. Make it energetic, funny, and non-gory.
- Keep anatomy clean and believable. Every human or animal should have the normal, correct number of visible limbs, digits, and joints for the pose. Do not generate extra arms, extra hands, fused limbs, duplicated body parts, or broken-looking anatomy.
- Preserve the physical scenario described by the winning joke. If the joke says a person is pinned, trapped, under, inside, holding, lifting, falling, carrying, or otherwise physically positioned in a specific way, show that exact physical relation clearly and safely instead of a nearby or symbolic version.
- If the joke describes someone pinned under a vehicle or other heavy object, show the person visibly underneath that object with their body position clear and cartoon-safe. Do not place them merely beside, near, or behind the object.
- Put a clean dark framed poster panel on the right side of the image. The panel should contain the winning joke text in large cream-white lettering with generous margins and legible line breaks.
Visible text allowed in the entire image: the right-panel joke text, a tiny stage sign reading Paperclipalypse, and optionally a small winner/title header above the panel.
Do not render layout words, percentages, prompt labels, section names, fake captions, signatures, watermarks, or filler microtext.
Optional small header text above the panel: Winner: Claude - Bleacher Utopia
Exact joke text to render in the right panel:
I went to my nephew’s t-ball game, and I swear the other parents have never been more alive. A woman behind me screamed, ‘HE WAS SAFE! HE WAS SO SAFE!’ about a six-year-old who was lying down in the infield, eating a dandelion. She’s not a mother. She’s a Shakespearean widow in a folding chair. I clap politely for everything, because I peaked emotionally at the snack table.
Scene source: use the exact winning joke text as the primary scene brief. The illustration must depict the concrete situation that the joke describes, not a softened, adjacent, or generic version. Do not infer a separate premise from all six seed terms.
Do not introduce unrelated seed-term concepts, occupations, animals, locations, props, or side characters unless they are explicitly required by the winning joke text.
If the winning joke mentions one seed-term concept but not another, depict only what the joke actually describes.
Round seed terms for exclusion reference only: Utopia, Fundraiser, Sporting Event Stands / Bleachers, War breaking out, Kind, Melodramatic. These are not scene ingredients unless the winning joke explicitly uses them.
Text rules: use simple clean lettering, spell every word correctly, keep the text inside the right panel, and do not distort letter shapes. The website HTML remains the canonical exact joke text if image lettering is imperfect.
The final image should feel like a finished feature image for an AI comedy tournament: funny, stylish, readable, full-color, and visually balanced across the paperclip comic, the joke scene, and the joke text.
